questions.question: Consider the statement “If my cricket team plays badly, they are not training enough”. Which one of the following statements is the contrapositive of the statement above?
questions.answer: The contrapositive of “if $P$ then $Q$” is “if not $Q$ then not $P$”. Here $P$: plays badly; $Q$: not training enough. Not $Q$ is “they are training enough” and not $P$ is “does not play badly”. So: if they are training enough, then the team does not play badly (B).
options: If they are not training enough, then my cricket team plays badly.
If they are training enough, then my cricket team does not play badly.
If my cricket team doesn’t play badly, then they are training enough.
If my cricket team plays badly, then they need more training.

questions.question: A particle of mass $m$ is moving horizontally in a straight line. Its motion is opposed by a force of magnitude $mkv+mkv^2$ newtons when its velocity is $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$, where $k$ is a positive constant. At time $t$ seconds the particle has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Which of the following is an expression for $x$ in terms of $v$?
questions.answer: $m\ddot x=-(mkv+mkv^2)=-mkv(1+v)$, so $\ddot x=-kv(1+v)$. Using $\ddot x=v\frac{dv}{dx}$: $v\frac{dv}{dx}=-kv(1+v)$, so $\frac{dv}{dx}=-k(1+v)$ and $\frac{dx}{dv}=-\frac{1}{k(1+v)}$. Therefore $x=-\frac1k\int\frac{dv}{1+v}$ (D).

questions.question: What is the principal argument of $\dfrac{-3\sqrt2-i\sqrt6}{2+2i}$?
questions.answer: The numerator $-3\sqrt2-i\sqrt6$ is in the third quadrant with reference angle $\tan^{-1}\frac{\sqrt6}{3\sqrt2}=\tan^{-1}\frac1{\sqrt3}=\frac\pi6$, so its principal argument is $-\pi+\frac\pi6=-\frac{5\pi}6$. The denominator $2+2i$ has argument $\frac\pi4$. Then $\arg=-\frac{5\pi}6-\frac\pi4=-\frac{13\pi}{12}$, which is outside $(-\pi,\pi]$, so add $2\pi$: $\frac{11\pi}{12}$ (C).

questions.question: If $i^n=p$, then what is a simplified expression in terms of $p$ for $i^{2n+3}$?
Which expression is equal to $\displaystyle\int3\sqrt x\,\ln x\,dx$?
questions.answer: By parts with $u=\ln x$, $v'=3\sqrt x$ (so $v=2x^{3/2}$): $\int3\sqrt x\ln x\,dx=2x\sqrt x\ln x-\int2\sqrt x\,dx=2x\sqrt x\ln x-\frac43x\sqrt x+C=2x\sqrt x\left(\ln x-\frac23\right)+C$ (A).

questions.question: If $\theta$ is the angle between $\mathbf a=\sqrt3\,\mathbf i+4\mathbf j-\mathbf k$ and $\mathbf b=\mathbf i-4\mathbf j+\sqrt3\,\mathbf k$, what is the value of $\cos(2\theta)$?
questions.answer: $\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b=\sqrt3-16-\sqrt3=-16$ and $|\mathbf a|=|\mathbf b|=\sqrt{20}$, so $\cos\theta=\frac{-16}{20}=-\frac45$. Then $\cos2\theta=2\cos^2\theta-1=2\cdot\frac{16}{25}-1=\frac7{25}$ (C).

questions.question: With a suitable substitution, which of the following is an equivalent expression to $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/3}\frac{\sec^2x\,dx}{\sec^2x-3\tan x+1}$?
questions.answer: Let $u=\tan x$, $du=\sec^2x\,dx$; $x=\frac\pi4\to u=1$ and $x=\frac\pi3\to u=\sqrt3$. Since $\sec^2x=1+u^2$, the denominator is $u^2-3u+2=(u-1)(u-2)$. Then $\frac1{(u-1)(u-2)}=\frac1{u-2}-\frac1{u-1}$ (partial fractions), so the integral is $\int_1^{\sqrt3}\left(\frac1{u-2}-\frac1{u-1}\right)du$ (C).

questions.question: The acceleration vector of a particle that starts from rest is given by $\mathbf a(t)=-4\sin(2t)\,\mathbf i+20\cos(2t)\,\mathbf j-20e^{-2t}\,\mathbf k$, where $t\ge0$. What is the velocity vector of the particle?
questions.answer: Integrate: $\mathbf v(t)=(2\cos2t+c_1)\,\mathbf i+(10\sin2t+c_2)\,\mathbf j+(10e^{-2t}+c_3)\,\mathbf k$. Starting from rest, $\mathbf v(0)=\mathbf 0$: $2+c_1=0$, $c_2=0$, $10+c_3=0$, so $c_1=-2$, $c_2=0$, $c_3=-10$. Hence $\mathbf v(t)=(2\cos2t-2)\,\mathbf i+10\sin2t\,\mathbf j+(10e^{-2t}-10)\,\mathbf k$ (B).

questions.question: A particle of mass $m$ kilograms hangs from a string that is attached to a fixed point. The particle is acted on by a horizontal force of magnitude $F$ newtons. The system is in equilibrium when the string makes an angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal, as shown in the diagram. The tension in the string has magnitude $T$ newtons. What is the value of $\tan\alpha$?
questions.answer: The tension acts along the string, up and to the left, at angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal. Resolve in equilibrium: vertically $T\sin\alpha=mg$; horizontally $T\cos\alpha=F$. Dividing: $\tan\alpha=\dfrac{mg}{F}$ (D).

questions.question: If the sum of two unit vectors $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$ is a unit vector, what is the magnitude of the difference of the two unit vectors $\mathbf u$ and $\mathbf v$?
questions.answer: $|\mathbf u+\mathbf v|^2=1$ gives $|\mathbf u|^2+2\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v+|\mathbf v|^2=1$, so $1+2\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v+1=1$ and $\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=-\frac12$. Then $|\mathbf u-\mathbf v|^2=1-2\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v+1=3$, so $|\mathbf u-\mathbf v|=\sqrt3$ (C).

questions.question: Let $z=1+i\sqrt3$. Express $z$ in modulus-argument form.
questions.answer: $|z|=\sqrt{1+3}=2$. $z$ is in the first quadrant with $\tan\theta=\sqrt3$, so $\theta=\frac\pi3$. Hence $z=2\left(\cos\frac\pi3+i\sin\frac\pi3\right)=2\operatorname{cis}\frac\pi3$.

questions.question: Let $z=1+i\sqrt3$. Hence, simplify $z^{10}+512z$.
questions.answer: With $z=2\operatorname{cis}\frac\pi3$, de Moivre gives $z^{10}=2^{10}\operatorname{cis}\frac{10\pi}3=1024\operatorname{cis}\frac{4\pi}3=1024\left(-\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}2i\right)=-512-512\sqrt3\,i$. Also $512z=512+512\sqrt3\,i$. Therefore $z^{10}+512z=0$.

questions.question: $ABCD$ is a parallelogram. Given that $\overrightarrow{AB}=6\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+3\mathbf k$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}=2\mathbf i+5\mathbf j+8\mathbf k$, find the size of angle $ABC$, giving your answer in degrees, to two decimal places.
questions.answer: Angle $ABC$ is the angle between $\overrightarrow{BA}=-\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-6\\2\\-3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\5\\8\end{pmatrix}$. $\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=-12+10-24=-26$, $|\overrightarrow{BA}|=\sqrt{36+4+9}=7$, $|\overrightarrow{BC}|=\sqrt{4+25+64}=\sqrt{93}$. So $\cos\angle ABC=\frac{-26}{7\sqrt{93}}$ and $\angle ABC\approx112.65^\circ$.

questions.question: Points $P$ and $Q$ represent the complex numbers $z$ and $w$ respectively in the complex plane. Triangle $OPQ$ is an equilateral triangle (see diagram; $Q$ is obtained from $P$ by a rotation about $O$ in the anticlockwise direction). Explain why $wz=z^2\operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac\pi3\right)$.
questions.answer: Since $\triangle OPQ$ is equilateral, $|w|=|z|$ and $\angle POQ=\frac\pi3$, with $Q$ anticlockwise from $P$. So $w$ is $z$ rotated through $\frac\pi3$ anticlockwise: $w=z\operatorname{cis}\frac\pi3$. Multiplying by $z$: $wz=z^2\operatorname{cis}\frac\pi3$.

questions.question: Points $P$ and $Q$ represent the complex numbers $z$ and $w$ respectively in the complex plane. Triangle $OPQ$ is an equilateral triangle (see diagram; $Q$ is obtained from $P$ by a rotation about $O$ in the anticlockwise direction). Given that $w=z\operatorname{cis}\left(\dfrac\pi3\right)$, prove that $z^2+w^2=zw$.
questions.answer: $z^2+w^2=z^2+z^2\operatorname{cis}\frac{2\pi}3=z^2\left(1+\cos\frac{2\pi}3+i\sin\frac{2\pi}3\right)=z^2\left(1-\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}2i\right)=z^2\left(\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}2i\right)=z^2\operatorname{cis}\frac\pi3=zw$.

questions.question: Find $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{1+2x-x^2}}$.
questions.answer: Complete the square: $1+2x-x^2=2-(x^2-2x+1)=2-(x-1)^2$. So $\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{2-(x-1)^2}}=\sin^{-1}\!\left(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt2}\right)+C$.

questions.question: The acceleration of a particle undergoing simple harmonic motion along the $x$-axis is given by $\ddot x=-4(x-3)$. Find the maximum speed of the particle if its speed as it passes through $x=1$ is $4\sqrt3$ metres per second.
questions.answer: $\ddot x=-n^2(x-c)$ with $n=2$ and centre $c=3$. Use $v\frac{dv}{dx}=-4(x-3)$: $\int_{4\sqrt3}^{v}v\,dv=-4\int_1^x(x-3)\,dx$, so $\frac{v^2}{2}-24=-4\left[\frac{x^2}2-3x\right]_1^x=-2x^2+12x-10$, giving $v^2=-4x^2+24x+28$. The maximum speed occurs at the centre $x=3$: $v^2=-36+72+28=64$, so the maximum speed is $\mathbf{8}$ m/s. (Alternatively $v^2=n^2[A^2-(x-3)^2]$: at $x=1$, $48=4(A^2-4)$, so $A=4$ and $v_{\max}=nA=8$.)

questions.question: Prove, by the method of contradiction, that there are no integers $a$ and $b$ which satisfy $a^2-8b=7$.
questions.answer: Assume there are integers $a$, $b$ with $a^2-8b=7$. Then $a^2=8b+7$ is odd (even + odd), so $a$ is odd: $a=2k+1$ for some integer $k$. Then $4k^2+4k+1=8b+7$, so $4k^2+4k-8b=6$, i.e. $2k^2+2k-4b=3$, so $2(k^2+k-2b)=3$. The left side is even and the right side is odd, a contradiction. Hence there are no integers $a$ and $b$ with $a^2-8b=7$.

questions.question: By integrating one of the two terms in the integrand by parts, or otherwise, find $\displaystyle\int\left(2\sqrt{1+x^3}+\frac{3x^3}{\sqrt{1+x^3}}\right)dx$.
questions.answer: Integrate $\frac{3x^3}{\sqrt{1+x^3}}=x\cdot\frac{3x^2}{\sqrt{1+x^3}}$ by parts with $u=x$, $v'=\frac{3x^2}{\sqrt{1+x^3}}$ so $v=2\sqrt{1+x^3}$: $\int\frac{3x^3}{\sqrt{1+x^3}}dx=2x\sqrt{1+x^3}-\int2\sqrt{1+x^3}\,dx$. Therefore $\int\left(2\sqrt{1+x^3}+\frac{3x^3}{\sqrt{1+x^3}}\right)dx=2x\sqrt{1+x^3}+C$. (Check: $\frac{d}{dx}\left(2x\sqrt{1+x^3}\right)=2\sqrt{1+x^3}+\frac{3x^3}{\sqrt{1+x^3}}$ ✓.)

questions.question: The line $l$ has equation $\dfrac{x-1}{h}=\dfrac{y-1}{3}=\dfrac{3-z}{6}$. Find the value(s) of $h$ for which the angle between $l$ and the $x$-axis is $120^\circ$.
questions.answer: Writing each ratio as $\lambda$: $x=1+h\lambda$, $y=1+3\lambda$, $z=3-6\lambda$, so $l$ has direction vector $\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}h\\3\\-6\end{pmatrix}$. With the $x$-axis taken in the direction $\mathbf i=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}$: $\mathbf d\cdot\mathbf i=|\mathbf d||\mathbf i|\cos120^\circ$, so $h=-\frac12\sqrt{h^2+45}$. Hence $-2h=\sqrt{h^2+45}$ (so $h<0$); squaring, $4h^2=h^2+45$, $h^2=15$, $h=-\sqrt{15}$. If instead the $x$-axis is taken in the direction $-\mathbf i$, the same working gives $h=+\sqrt{15}$. So $h=\pm\sqrt{15}$ (the paper’s solution accepts both, $h=-\sqrt{15}$ corresponding to the direction $\mathbf i$).

questions.question: Show that $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3}\frac1{1+\sin x}\,dx=4-2\sqrt3$.
questions.answer: Multiply by $\frac{1-\sin x}{1-\sin x}$: $\frac1{1+\sin x}=\frac{1-\sin x}{1-\sin^2x}=\frac{1-\sin x}{\cos^2x}=\sec^2x-\sin x\cos^{-2}x$. Antiderivative: $\tan x-\sec x$ (since $\frac{d}{dx}\sec x=\sec x\tan x=\sin x\cos^{-2}x$). So the integral is $\left[\tan x-\frac1{\cos x}\right]_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3}=\left(-\sqrt3+2\right)-\left(\sqrt3-2\right)=4-2\sqrt3$. (Alternatively use $t=\tan\frac x2$.)

questions.question: Given that $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3}\frac1{1+\sin x}\,dx=4-2\sqrt3$, hence find the exact value of $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3}\frac{x}{1+\sin x}\,dx$.
questions.answer: Let $J=\int_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3}\frac{x}{1+\sin x}\,dx$ and substitute $u=\pi-x$: $du=-dx$, limits $\frac{2\pi}3\to\frac\pi3$ and $\frac\pi3\to\frac{2\pi}3$, and $\sin(\pi-u)=\sin u$. So $J=\int_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3}\frac{\pi-u}{1+\sin u}\,du=\pi\int_{\pi/3}^{2\pi/3}\frac{du}{1+\sin u}-J$. Hence $2J=\pi(4-2\sqrt3)$ and $J=\pi(2-\sqrt3)$.

questions.question: The vertices of triangle $OAB$ have coordinates $A(6,-18,-6)$, $B(7,-1,3)$, where $O$ is a fixed origin. The point $N$ lies on $OA$ so that $ON:NA=1:2$. The point $M$ is the midpoint of $OB$. The point $P$ is the intersection of $AM$ and $BN$. By using vector methods, determine the coordinates of $P$.
questions.answer: Let $\mathbf a=\overrightarrow{OA}=(6,-18,-6)$ and $\mathbf b=\overrightarrow{OB}=(7,-1,3)$. Then $\overrightarrow{ON}=\frac13\mathbf a$ and $\overrightarrow{OM}=\frac12\mathbf b$. $P$ lies on $BN$: $\overrightarrow{OP}=\mathbf b+s\left(\frac13\mathbf a-\mathbf b\right)=\frac s3\mathbf a+(1-s)\mathbf b$. $P$ also lies on $AM$: $\overrightarrow{OP}=\mathbf a+t\left(\frac12\mathbf b-\mathbf a\right)=(1-t)\mathbf a+\frac t2\mathbf b$. Since $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are not parallel, equate coefficients: $\frac s3=1-t$ and $1-s=\frac t2$. From the second, $t=2-2s$; substituting, $\frac s3=2s-1$, so $s=\frac35$ and $t=\frac45$. Therefore $\overrightarrow{OP}=\frac15\mathbf a+\frac25\mathbf b=\frac15(6,-18,-6)+\frac25(7,-1,3)=(4,-4,0)$. So $P=(4,-4,0)$.

questions.question: Prove, **without** the use of mathematical induction, that $5^{2n}-1$ is divisible by 8 for all positive integers $n$.
questions.answer: $5^{2n}-1=25^n-1$. Using $a^n-b^n=(a-b)\left(a^{n-1}+a^{n-2}b+\dots+b^{n-1}\right)$ with $a=25$, $b=1$: $25^n-1=24\left(25^{n-1}+25^{n-2}+\dots+25+1\right)$, which is $24$ times an integer, hence a multiple of 8. (Alternatively $5^{2n}-1=(5^n-1)(5^n+1)$ is a product of two consecutive even numbers, one of which is a multiple of 4, so the product is divisible by 8.)

questions.question: A particle of mass 1 kg is projected vertically upwards with an initial velocity of $100\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in a medium in which the resistance force is equal to $0.01$ times the square of the particle’s velocity, that is $0.01v^2$. Use $g=10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Show that the maximum height reached by the particle is $50\log_e11$ metres.
questions.answer: Take upwards as positive. Going up, gravity and resistance both act downwards: $\ddot x=-10-0.01v^2=-\frac{1000+v^2}{100}$. With $\ddot x=v\frac{dv}{dx}$: $\frac{v\,dv}{1000+v^2}=-\frac{1}{100}dx$. At maximum height $H$, $v=0$: $\int_{100}^{0}\frac{v\,dv}{1000+v^2}=-\frac1{100}\int_0^Hdx$, so $\frac12\left[\ln(1000+v^2)\right]_{100}^0=-\frac H{100}$, giving $H=50\left[\ln11000-\ln1000\right]=50\ln\frac{11000}{1000}=50\ln11$ metres.

questions.question: A particle of mass 1 kg is projected vertically upwards with an initial velocity of $100\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ in a medium in which the resistance force is equal to $0.01$ times the square of the particle’s velocity, that is $0.01v^2$. Use $g=10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. The maximum height reached is $50\ln11$ metres. Calculate the downward velocity of the particle on its return to the point of projection. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
questions.answer: Coming down (take downwards as positive, $x$ measured down from the top): $\ddot x=10-0.01v^2=\frac{1000-v^2}{100}$, so $\frac{v\,dv}{1000-v^2}=\frac{dx}{100}$. From rest at the top ($v=0$) to the point of projection ($x=50\ln11$), with final speed $V$: $-\frac12\left[\ln(1000-v^2)\right]_0^V=\frac{50\ln11}{100}$, so $-\frac12\ln\frac{1000-V^2}{1000}=\frac12\ln11$, giving $\frac{1000-V^2}{1000}=\frac1{11}$. Then $V^2=1000-\frac{1000}{11}=\frac{10000}{11}\approx909.09$ and $V\approx30.15$ m/s downward.

questions.question: A polynomial is given by $P(z)=z^4-6z^3+38z^2-94z+221$. Given that $z=2+3i$ is a root of the equation $P(z)=0$, find the three other roots of $P(z)=0$.
questions.answer: $P$ has real coefficients, so $2-3i$ is also a root. Let the other two roots be $\alpha,\beta$. Sum of roots: $\alpha+\beta+(2+3i)+(2-3i)=6$, so $\alpha+\beta=2$. Product of roots: $\alpha\beta(2+3i)(2-3i)=221$, so $13\alpha\beta=221$ and $\alpha\beta=17$. Then $\alpha$ satisfies $\alpha+\frac{17}\alpha=2$, i.e. $\alpha^2-2\alpha+17=0$, so $\alpha=\frac{2\pm\sqrt{-64}}2=1\pm4i$. The other three roots are $2-3i$, $1+4i$ and $1-4i$.

questions.question: If $z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)$, use de Moivre’s theorem to solve the complex equation $z^5=\overline z$. Express your answer(s) in the form $a+ib$.
questions.answer: $\overline z=r\operatorname{cis}(-\theta)$ and $z^5=r^5\operatorname{cis}5\theta$. Equate moduli: $r^5=r$, so $r(r^4-1)=0$, giving $r=0$ or $r=1$ (as $r\ge0$). Equate arguments: $5\theta=-\theta+2k\pi$, so $6\theta=2k\pi$ and $\theta=\frac{k\pi}3$. For $r=1$: $k=0$: $z=1$; $k=1$: $z=\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}2i$; $k=2$: $z=-\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}2i$; $k=3$: $z=-1$; $k=-2$: $z=-\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}2i$; $k=-1$: $z=\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}2i$. Together with $r=0$: the solutions are $z=0$, $\pm1$, $\pm\frac12\pm\frac{\sqrt3}2i$ (all four sign combinations).

questions.question: Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int\operatorname{cosec}^nx\,dx$ for integers $n\ge0$. Show that $I_n=\dfrac{-\cot x\operatorname{cosec}^{n-2}x}{n-1}+\dfrac{n-2}{n-1}I_{n-2}$ for integers $n\ge2$.
questions.answer: Write $\operatorname{cosec}^nx=\operatorname{cosec}^{n-2}x\cdot\operatorname{cosec}^2x$ and integrate by parts with $u=\operatorname{cosec}^{n-2}x$, $v'=\operatorname{cosec}^2x$. Then $u'=-(n-2)\operatorname{cosec}^{n-2}x\cot x$ and $v=-\cot x$. $I_n=-\cot x\operatorname{cosec}^{n-2}x-(n-2)\int\operatorname{cosec}^{n-2}x\cot^2x\,dx$. Use $\cot^2x=\operatorname{cosec}^2x-1$: $I_n=-\cot x\operatorname{cosec}^{n-2}x-(n-2)(I_n-I_{n-2})$. So $(n-1)I_n=-\cot x\operatorname{cosec}^{n-2}x+(n-2)I_{n-2}$, giving $I_n=\frac{-\cot x\operatorname{cosec}^{n-2}x}{n-1}+\frac{n-2}{n-1}I_{n-2}$.

questions.question: Let $I_n=\displaystyle\int\operatorname{cosec}^nx\,dx$, where $I_n=\dfrac{-\cot x\operatorname{cosec}^{n-2}x}{n-1}+\dfrac{n-2}{n-1}I_{n-2}$ for $n\ge2$. Hence evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/6}^{5\pi/6}\operatorname{cosec}^4x\,dx$.
questions.answer: With $n=4$: $I_4=-\frac{\cot x\operatorname{cosec}^2x}3+\frac23I_2$ and $I_2=\int\operatorname{cosec}^2x\,dx=-\cot x$. Evaluate between $\frac\pi6$ and $\frac{5\pi}6$, using $\cot\frac\pi6=\sqrt3$, $\cot\frac{5\pi}6=-\sqrt3$, $\operatorname{cosec}^2=4$ at both: $\left[-\frac{\cot x\operatorname{cosec}^2x}3\right]=\frac{4\sqrt3}3-\left(-\frac{4\sqrt3}3\right)=\frac{8\sqrt3}3$ and $\frac23\left[-\cot x\right]=\frac23(\sqrt3+\sqrt3)=\frac{4\sqrt3}3$. Total: $\frac{8\sqrt3}3+\frac{4\sqrt3}3=4\sqrt3$.

questions.question: A train of mass $m$, pulled by a locomotive which exerts a constant (propelling) force $P$, is moving at speed $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ along a straight level track against a resistive force $mkv$, where $k$ is a positive constant. The speed increases from $2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ to $4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ over a time interval of 5 seconds. Show that $P=2km\left(\dfrac{2e^{5k}-1}{e^{5k}-1}\right)$.
questions.answer: $m\frac{dv}{dt}=P-mkv$, so $\int_2^4\frac{m\,dv}{P-mkv}=\int_0^5dt=5$. Then $-\frac1k\left[\ln|P-mkv|\right]_2^4=5$, so $\ln\left|\frac{P-4mk}{P-2mk}\right|=-5k$. Since $P>mkv$ throughout (the train is accelerating), $\frac{P-2mk}{P-4mk}=e^{5k}$. Then $P-2mk=e^{5k}(P-4mk)$, so $P(e^{5k}-1)=4mke^{5k}-2mk=2mk(2e^{5k}-1)$ and $P=2km\left(\dfrac{2e^{5k}-1}{e^{5k}-1}\right)$.

questions.question: A train of mass $m$, pulled by a locomotive which exerts a constant (propelling) force $P$, is moving at speed $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ along a straight level track against a resistive force $mkv$, where $k$ is a positive constant. The speed increases from $2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ to $4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ over a time interval of 5 seconds. Given that $P=2km\left(\dfrac{2e^{5k}-1}{e^{5k}-1}\right)$, find the corresponding distance moved.
questions.answer: Use $mv\frac{dv}{dx}=P-mkv$: $\int_2^4\frac{mv\,dv}{P-mkv}=\int_0^{d}dx=d$. Write $\frac{mv}{P-mkv}=-\frac1k+\frac{P}{k(P-mkv)}$. Then $d=\left[-\frac vk\right]_2^4+\frac Pk\left[-\frac1{mk}\ln|P-mkv|\right]_2^4=-\frac2k-\frac{P}{mk^2}\ln\left|\frac{P-4mk}{P-2mk}\right|=\frac{P}{mk^2}\ln\frac{P-2mk}{P-4mk}-\frac2k$. From part (i), $\frac{P-2mk}{P-4mk}=e^{5k}$, so $d=\frac{5P}{mk}-\frac2k=\dfrac{10\left(2e^{5k}-1\right)}{e^{5k}-1}-\dfrac2k$ metres.

questions.question: A train of mass $m$, pulled by a locomotive which exerts a constant (propelling) force $P$, is moving at speed $v\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ along a straight level track against a resistive force $mkv$, where $k$ is a positive constant. The speed increases from $2\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ to $4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ over a time interval of 5 seconds. There is an upper bound to the speed that the train can attain. Find the value of this upper bound. (Use $P=2km\left(\frac{2e^{5k}-1}{e^{5k}-1}\right)$.)
questions.answer: The speed is bounded when the acceleration is zero: $0=P-mkv$, so $v=\frac{P}{mk}=\dfrac{2\left(2e^{5k}-1\right)}{e^{5k}-1}$ m/s.

questions.question: Use the principle of mathematical induction to prove that $3^n>n^3$ for all integers $n>3$.
questions.answer: **Base case** $n=4$: $3^4=81>64=4^3$ ✓. **Assume** $3^k>k^3$ for some integer $k\ge4$. **Prove** $3^{k+1}>(k+1)^3$. $3^{k+1}=3\cdot3^k>3k^3$ (by the assumption). Now $3k^3-(k+1)^3=2k^3-3k^2-3k-1=(k-1)^3+k(k^2-6)>0$ for $k\ge4$ (since $(k-1)^3>0$ and $k^2-6>0$). So $3^{k+1}>3k^3>(k+1)^3$. Hence if true for $n=k$ then true for $n=k+1$; as it is true for $n=4$, it is true for all integers $n>3$ by induction.

questions.question:
Let $S$ be a sphere with the centre at $\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}$ and radius $r=5$. A line $l$ is defined by the parametric equation $\mathbf r(\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}-7\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}$, where $\lambda\in\mathbb R$.

Find the point(s) of intersection between the line and the sphere.
questions.answer: Points on the line: $(3-7\lambda,\,4-\lambda,\,0)$. On the sphere: $(3-7\lambda)^2+(4-\lambda)^2=25$, so $9-42\lambda+49\lambda^2+16-8\lambda+\lambda^2=25$, i.e. $50\lambda^2-50\lambda=0$, $\lambda(\lambda-1)=0$. So $\lambda=0$ or $\lambda=1$, giving the points $(3,4,0)$ and $(-4,3,0)$.

questions.question:
Let $S$ be a sphere with the centre at $\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\\0\end{pmatrix}$ and radius $r=5$. A line $l$ is defined by the parametric equation $\mathbf r(\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}-7\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}$, where $\lambda\in\mathbb R$.

Find the shortest distance from the centre of the sphere to the line.
questions.answer: The line meets the sphere at $A(3,4,0)$ and $B(-4,3,0)$, so the perpendicular from the centre $O$ meets the chord $AB$ at its midpoint $M$. $|AB|=\sqrt{49+1}=5\sqrt2$, so $AM=\frac{5\sqrt2}2$. Then $OM=\sqrt{OA^2-AM^2}=\sqrt{25-\frac{25}2}=\dfrac{5\sqrt2}2\approx3.54$. (Check: $\overrightarrow{OA}\cdot\mathbf d$ projection: the component of $\overrightarrow{AO}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-4\\0\end{pmatrix}$ along $\mathbf d=\begin{pmatrix}-7\\-1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ is $\frac{21+4}{\sqrt{50}}=\frac{5\sqrt2}2$ along the chord, giving $AM=\frac{5\sqrt2}2$ as above.)

questions.question: The points $A$, $B$ and $C$ represent the complex numbers $z_1$, $z_2$ and $z_3$ respectively on the Argand diagram. Prove that if $\dfrac{z_2-z_3}{z_1-z_3}=\dfrac{z_1-z_3}{z_1-z_2}$, then triangle $ABC$ is an equilateral triangle.
questions.answer: Let $a=z_1-z_2$, $b=z_2-z_3$, $c=z_3-z_1$, so $a+b+c=0$. The given relation is $\frac{b}{-c}=\frac{-c}{a}$, i.e. $ab=c^2$. Substitute $c=-(a+b)$: $ab=(a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2$, so $a^2+ab+b^2=0$, i.e. $\left(\frac ab\right)^2+\frac ab+1=0$. Hence $\frac ab=\operatorname{cis}\left(\pm\frac{2\pi}3\right)=\omega$, a complex number of modulus 1, so $|a|=|b|$. Then $c=-(a+b)=-b(1+\omega)=-b\cdot(-\omega^2)=b\omega^2$ (using $1+\omega+\omega^2=0$), so $|c|=|b|$. Thus $|z_1-z_2|=|z_2-z_3|=|z_3-z_1|$, i.e. $AB=BC=CA$ and triangle $ABC$ is equilateral.

questions.question: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int\frac{\ln x}{(1+\ln x)^2}\,dx$.
questions.answer: Write $\frac{\ln x}{(1+\ln x)^2}=\frac{1}{1+\ln x}-\frac{1}{(1+\ln x)^2}$ and integrate $\int\frac{dx}{1+\ln x}$ by parts with $u=\frac1{1+\ln x}$, $v'=1$: $u'=-\frac{1}{x(1+\ln x)^2}$, $v=x$, so $\int\frac{dx}{1+\ln x}=\frac{x}{1+\ln x}+\int\frac{dx}{(1+\ln x)^2}$. Therefore $\int\frac{\ln x}{(1+\ln x)^2}dx=\dfrac{x}{1+\ln x}+C$. (Check: $\frac{d}{dx}\frac{x}{1+\ln x}=\frac{(1+\ln x)-1}{(1+\ln x)^2}=\frac{\ln x}{(1+\ln x)^2}$ ✓.)

questions.question: It is given that for any three positive numbers $x$, $y$ and $z$ it can be shown that $(x+y)(x+z)(y+z)\ge8xyz$. Use this result to prove that if $a$, $b$ and $c$ are any three positive numbers such that each number is less than the sum of the other two, then $(a+b-c)(b+c-a)(c+a-b)\le abc$.
questions.answer: Since each number is less than the sum of the other two, $a+b-c>0$, $b+c-a>0$ and $c+a-b>0$. Let $x=a+b-c$, $y=a+c-b$, $z=b+c-a$ (all positive). Then $x+y=2a$, $x+z=2b$, $y+z=2c$. The given result gives $(2a)(2b)(2c)\ge8(a+b-c)(a+c-b)(b+c-a)$, i.e. $8abc\ge8(a+b-c)(a+c-b)(b+c-a)$. Hence $(a+b-c)(b+c-a)(c+a-b)\le abc$.

questions.question: Let $S=(\sqrt{50}+7)^{2000}+(\sqrt{50}-7)^{2000}$. Prove that $S$ is an even integer.
questions.answer: By the binomial theorem, $(\sqrt{50}+7)^{2000}=\sum_{r=0}^{2000}\binom{2000}{r}(\sqrt{50})^{2000-r}7^r$ and $(\sqrt{50}-7)^{2000}=\sum_{r=0}^{2000}\binom{2000}{r}(\sqrt{50})^{2000-r}(-7)^r$. Adding, the terms with odd $r$ cancel and the terms with even $r$ double: $S=2\sum_{k=0}^{1000}\binom{2000}{2k}(\sqrt{50})^{2000-2k}7^{2k}=2\sum_{k=0}^{1000}\binom{2000}{2k}50^{1000-k}7^{2k}$. Each term is an integer (the exponent of $\sqrt{50}$ is even), so $S=2\times$(an integer), an even integer.

questions.question: Without the use of a calculator, show that $0<\sqrt{50}-7<0.1$. (You may use the fact that $71^2=5041$.)

Let $S=(\sqrt{50}+7)^{2000}+(\sqrt{50}-7)^{2000}$, which is an even integer, and $0<\sqrt{50}-7<0.1$. Hence, or otherwise, prove that the first two thousand digits after the decimal point in the decimal expansion of $(\sqrt{50}+7)^{2000}$ are all the digit 9.
questions.answer: $(\sqrt{50}+7)^{2000}=S-(\sqrt{50}-7)^{2000}$. Since $0<\sqrt{50}-7<0.1=10^{-1}$, we have $0<(\sqrt{50}-7)^{2000}<10^{-2000}$. So $(\sqrt{50}+7)^{2000}=S-\varepsilon$ with $S$ an integer and $0<\varepsilon<10^{-2000}$. Therefore the number is just below the integer $S$: its fractional part is $1-\varepsilon=0.\underbrace{99\ldots9}_{\ge2000}\ldots$ (since $1-\varepsilon>1-10^{-2000}=0.\underbrace{9\ldots9}_{2000}$). So the first 2000 digits after the decimal point are all 9.

questions.question:
The diagram shows the graph of $y=\dfrac{e^x}{x}$.

Find the coordinates of the stationary point.
questions.answer: $y=\frac{e^x}x$, so $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{xe^x-e^x}{x^2}=\frac{e^x(x-1)}{x^2}$. Stationary points occur when $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$: $x=1$ (as $e^x\ne0$), and $y=\frac e1=e$. The stationary point is $(1,e)$ (a minimum, as $\frac{dy}{dx}<0$ for $0<x<1$ and $>0$ for $x>1$).

questions.question: Find $a$ if $\displaystyle\int_a^{2a}\frac{e^x}{x}\,dx=\int_a^{2a}\frac{e^x}{x^2}\,dx$.
questions.answer: Move to one side: $\int_a^{2a}\left(\frac{e^x}x-\frac{e^x}{x^2}\right)dx=0$, i.e. $\int_a^{2a}\frac{xe^x-e^x}{x^2}dx=0$. The integrand is $\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{e^x}x\right)$ (from part (i)), so $\left[\frac{e^x}x\right]_a^{2a}=0$: $\frac{e^{2a}}{2a}-\frac{e^a}a=0$, so $e^{2a}=2e^a$, $e^a=2$ and $a=\ln2$.

questions.question: The diagram shows the graph of $y=\dfrac{e^x}{x}$. Hence, or otherwise, show that it is not possible to find distinct integers $m$ and $n$ such that $\displaystyle\int_m^n\frac{e^x}{x}\,dx=\int_m^n\frac{e^x}{x^2}\,dx$.
questions.answer: As in part (ii), $\int_m^n\left(\frac{e^x}x-\frac{e^x}{x^2}\right)dx=\left[\frac{e^x}x\right]_m^n$, so the equality requires $\frac{e^n}n=\frac{e^m}m$ (the integrals only exist if $m,n$ are non-zero and of the same sign, since the integrand has a discontinuity at $x=0$). Suppose $m\ne n$ are integers with $f(m)=f(n)$ where $f(x)=\frac{e^x}x$. From the graph, $f$ is strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,0)$ and on $(0,1)$ and strictly increasing on $(1,\infty)$, with minimum $f(1)=e$. So $f(m)=f(n)$ for distinct $m,n$ of the same sign is only possible if one lies in $(0,1)$ and the other in $(1,\infty)$ (on the negative axis $f$ is one-to-one, and on $[1,\infty)$ it is one-to-one). But there is no integer in the interval $(0,1)$, a contradiction. Hence no such distinct integers exist.
